content.intro: This lesson introduces removing sensitive data from history as part of Git Security and Professional Best Practices. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: History rewriting can remove sensitive content from reachable history in a carefully controlled process, but it cannot guarantee deletion from every clone, cache or backup. Credential rotation and incident response remain essential.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** History rewriting can remove sensitive content from reachable history in a carefully controlled process, but it cannot guarantee deletion from every clone, cache or backup. Credential rotation and incident response remain essential.

For **Removing Sensitive Data from History**, keep the named subtopics in view: Why deleting a file in a new commit is insufficient; History-rewriting concepts; Coordinating rewritten history with collaborators; Rotating exposed credentials. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Use a fake sample filename. If a real secret was exposed, revoke/rotate it first; later deletion does not erase older copies, clones or remote refs.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
